title: Electrical Conductivity
short_intro: Electrical conductivity is the measure of a material's ability to conduct an electric current, defined as the reciprocal of electrical resistivity. In microscopic terms, it is determined by the density of mobile charge carriers, their elementary charge, and their drift mobility within the medium.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of conductivity and resistivity, Ohm's law in vector form (J = sigma E), temperature dependence of resistance and resistivity for metals and semiconductors, color coding of carbon resistors, and grouping of resistances.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Drude model derivation of conductivity, relaxation time of electrons, microscopic interpretation of mobility, tensor conductivity in anisotropic media, and AC response involving complex permittivity and conductivity.

prerequisites: Current density and drift velocity of electrons
Basic thermal physics and carrier statistics

concept_notes.heading: Microscopic Definition and Vector Form of Ohm's Law
bullets: Conductivity (sigma) is defined as the inverse of electrical resistivity (rho), such that sigma = 1 / rho.
Ohm's law in microscopic form relates the current density J to the electric field E via the relation J = sigma E.
The SI unit of electrical conductivity is Siemens per meter (S/m) or ohm<sup>-1</sup>m<sup>-1</sup>.

concept_notes.heading: Drude Model of Conduction in Metals
bullets: Metals possess a high density of free conduction electrons that move randomly and collide periodically with fixed ionic cores.
Under an applied electric field E, electrons acquire a net directional drift velocity vd superimposed on their random thermal motion.
The average time interval between successive collisions is known as the relaxation time (tau).

concept_notes.heading: Temperature Dependence of Conductivity
bullets: For metallic conductors, conductivity decreases with an increase in temperature due to enhanced thermal vibrations of ions reducing the relaxation time tau.
For intrinsic semiconductors and insulators, conductivity increases exponentially with temperature as more covalent bonds are thermally broken to release charge carriers.
The temperature coefficient of resistivity (alpha) is positive for pure metals and negative for semiconductors and carbon.

concept_notes.heading: Carrier Mobility and Conductivity
bullets: Mobility (mu) is defined as the magnitude of drift velocity acquired per unit electric field, mu = |vd| / E.
Total conductivity in semiconductors involves contributions from both negatively charged electrons and positively charged holes: sigma = e (n mu_n + p mu_p).
In pure (intrinsic) semiconductors, the electron concentration n equals the hole concentration p, equaling the intrinsic carrier concentration ni.

derivations.title: Drude Model Derivation of Electrical Conductivity
derivations.conditions: Steady uniform electric field applied to a metal containing free electrons of mass m and charge e
steps: Write the equation of motion for a conduction electron between collisions: m(dvd/dt) = -eE - m(vd/tau), where tau is the relaxation time.
Under steady-state conditions, the acceleration is zero (dvd/dt = 0), yielding the drift velocity: vd = -(e tau / m) E.
Relate current density J to drift velocity and carrier density n: J = -n e vd = (ne<sup>2</sup> tau / m) E.
Compare with the microscopic Ohm's law J = sigma E to identify the expression for conductivity.

derivations.title: Temperature Dependence of Resistivity
derivations.conditions: Small temperature variations where linear approximation holds
steps: Express resistivity rho at temperature T as a linear perturbation from a reference temperature T_0: rho(T) = rho_0 [1 + alpha (T - T_0)].
Define the temperature coefficient of resistivity alpha as the fractional change in resistivity per unit change in temperature: alpha =  rac{1}{ho_0}  rac{dho}{dT}.
Substitute rho = m / (n e^2 tau) into the definition to observe how collision frequency and thermal expansion affect alpha in metals.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Resistivity vs Temperature for Metals
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of resistivity (rho) on the y-axis against absolute temperature (T) on the x-axis, showing a nearly linear increase at high temperatures and a non-linear drop towards zero near absolute zero.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: At high temperatures, phonon scattering dominates, making resistivity proportional to T. At very low temperatures, impurity scattering dictates residual resistivity.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct identification questions on metallic behavior vs temperature and intercept interpretations.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Resistivity vs Temperature for Semiconductors
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A steeply decaying exponential curve plotting resistivity versus temperature.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Thermal excitation exponentially increases carrier density n, overpowering the decrease in relaxation time, causing rapid drop in resistivity.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Distinguishing semiconductor thermal properties from metallic properties in assertion-reasoning items.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Current Density vs Electric Field (Ohmic vs Non-Ohmic)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line passing through the origin for ohmic conductors, and a curved/saturating profile for non-ohmic devices like diodes or electrolytes.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the J-E curve yields the electrical conductivity sigma for linear media.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Graphical determination of conductivity values and breakdown conditions.

solved_numericals.question: A silver wire has a resistivity of 1.6 x 10<sup>-8</sup> ohm·m at 20&deg;C. Calculate its electrical conductivity.
solution_steps: Recall the relation between conductivity and resistivity: sigma = 1 / rho.
Substitute the given value of rho = 1.6 x 10<sup>-8</sup> ohm·m.
Calculate the reciprocal: sigma = 1 / (1.6 x 10<sup>-8</sup>) = 0.625 x 10<sup>8</sup> = 6.25 x 10<sup>7</sup> S/m.

solved_numericals.question: In a doped silicon semiconductor, the concentration of electrons is 2 x 10<sup>19</sup> m<sup>-3</sup> and holes is 1 x 10<sup>18</sup> m<sup>-3</sup>. Given the electron mobility is 0.13 m<sup>2</sup>/(V·s) and hole mobility is 0.05 m<sup>2</sup>/(V·s), find the total electrical conductivity.
solution_steps: Use the formula for semiconductor conductivity: sigma = e (n mu_n + p mu_p).
Substitute values: e = 1.6 x 10<sup>-19</sup> C, n = 2 x 10<sup>19</sup>, mu_n = 0.13, p = 1 x 10<sup>18</sup>, mu_p = 0.05.
Calculate electron contribution: 1.6 x 10<sup>-19</sup> x (2 x 10<sup>19</sup> x 0.13) = 1.6 x 2 x 0.13 = 0.416 S/m.
Calculate hole contribution: 1.6 x 10<sup>-19</sup> x (1 x 10<sup>18</sup> x 0.05) = 1.6 x 0.1 x 0.05 = 0.008 S/m.

solved_numericals.question: Assuming each copper atom contributes one free electron, calculate the conductivity of copper at room temperature. Given: density of copper = 8960 kg/m<sup>3</sup>, atomic mass = 63.5 g/mol, relaxation time tau = 2.5 x 10<sup>-14</sup> s, mass of electron = 9.1 x 10<sup>-31</sup> kg, and Avogadro number = 6.023 x 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>.
solution_steps: Find electron number density n = (Density x Avogadro number) / (Atomic mass).
n = (8960 x 6.023 x 10<sup>23</sup>) / (63.5 x 10<sup>-3</sup>) approx 8.5 x 10<sup>28</sup> m<sup>-3</sup>.
Apply Drude formula: sigma = (n e^2 tau) / m.
sigma = (8.5 x 10<sup>28</sup> x (1.6 x 10<sup>-19</sup>)<sup>2</sup> x 2.5 x 10<sup>-14</sup>) / (9.1 x 10<sup>-31</sup>).
Evaluate numerical result: sigma approx 6.0 x 10<sup>7</sup> S/m.

assumptions_and_limitations: The Drude model assumes electrons act as a classical ideal gas, ignoring quantum mechanical Fermi-Dirac statistics and Pauli exclusion principle.
Relaxation time tau is treated as a constant independent of electron velocity and energy, which is an approximation valid only near thermal equilibrium.

common_misconceptions.wrong: High conductivity implies that electrons travel through a wire at very high speeds.
common_misconceptions.correct: Drift velocity of electrons is extremely small (on the order of mm/s), but the electric field propagates at nearly the speed of light.
common_misconceptions.why: The electrical signal travels via electromagnetic wave propagation rather than individual electron transit.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Semiconductors have a positive temperature coefficient of resistivity like metals.
common_misconceptions.correct: Semiconductors have a negative temperature coefficient of resistivity.
common_misconceptions.why: Thermal generation of additional charge carriers outweighs the decrease in relaxation time at higher temperatures.

quick_revision: Conductivity is the reciprocal of resistivity: sigma = 1 / rho with SI unit S/m.
Microscopic Ohm's law is expressed as J = sigma E.
Drude model formula for metals is sigma = ne<sup>2</sup>tau / m.
Metals exhibit a positive temperature coefficient of resistivity, whereas semiconductors exhibit a negative coefficient.
